rv.q: It's a shocking and cynical final flourish to rival anything created by Le Carré.
The result is intimate and disturbing.

While undeniably intriguing, at 65 minutes it feels too cryptic for its mighty subject and, since we listen to the dialogue through headphones and view the action through a glass fourth wall, there is a double sense of detachment.
Natalie Abrahami's production feels polished and flashy: a machine that works, but holds us at arm's length from these characters.
If you don't care about historical and national anachronism, about verbal tone, this staging will delight — if you do, your pleasure might be compromised.

cn.t: An innovative audio experiment set in 1968 East Berlin divides critics: some praise its terrific sound design and intrigue, while others find it too cryptic and detached, with unconvincing dialogue undermining the premise.
